memories.content: Complete the problem framing within the first two sentences so the reader reaches the proposal's central issue before any supporting background.
Use the first sentence for the concrete problem and the second for its consequence; reserve later sentences for the proposed response.
Specify the user, context, and interaction to be explored in the primary HCI research question.
Provide one compact visual summary when proposing an unfamiliar interaction procedure.
Mark the conditions that move an unfamiliar interaction procedure from one step to the next in its visual summary.
Present the master’s research schedule as phased periods for exploration, design, prototyping, and user evaluation.
Link one reviewable deliverable to each phase of the master’s research.
Place the gap left by HCI-related research and the proposed design and empirical contributions in close proximity.
Divide a two-page proposal with short descriptive subheadings so a reader can jump directly to the problem, proposed response, and next steps.
Give the problem and proposed response their own descriptive subheadings instead of relying only on paragraph transitions.
Give the next steps and requested support their own descriptive subheading so they remain easy to find on a return visit.
Place pilot observation or initial prototype results near sentences supporting feasibility claims.
Readers often decide what a proposal is about from its first two sentences before scanning the rest of the page.
When setup continues past the second sentence, readers who are skimming often retain the background topic but miss the exact problem being proposed.
Reuse the same short subheadings in discussion so a reader can return to a section without searching through the whole page.
Use visible subheadings as a completeness check: an empty or missing section makes an omitted part of the proposal immediately apparent.
Readers often scan section labels before deciding which paragraph to read closely.
Specify field and user data sources and analysis procedures corresponding to all HCI research questions.
In preregistered studies, clarify the criteria for judging plan changes.
In preregistered studies, clarify the location for recording plan changes.
Use a justified minimum-to-maximum target range when confirmations can change, and tie the minimum and maximum to different workload and budget cases.
Specify the observation records, system logs, or interview tools used to collect each type of field and user data.
Specify whether each type of field and user data will be collected before, during, or after deployment.
Readers cannot assess a target range unless both bounds have a stated consequence for schedule, workload, or cost.
In field deployments, network and service instability exist as independent causes of task failure alongside design choices.
If a safety signal occurs in the field system, existing institutional safety procedures take precedence over the research schedule and data collection plan.
Reviewers judge answerability by tracing the path from each research question to its data sources and analysis procedures.
The user authoring this proposal tends to present implemented feature lists directly as design contributions.
Define what can still be completed at the minimum target instead of treating every number inside the range as operationally identical.
Use a bounded range to absorb expected confirmation changes without pretending that one early estimate is guaranteed.
Show how session count and facilitator time change at the minimum and maximum bounds.
Define the additional workload or deliverable enabled at the maximum target so the upper bound is not an arbitrary cushion.
A bounded range preserves uncertainty honestly but makes the final workload and budget less certain than one fixed target.

analysis.overview: The frames emphasize complementary but separate dimensions of proposal quality. The reference frame focuses on concise framing, visual explanation, scheduling, contribution placement, navigation, and feasibility evidence; the compared frame focuses on methodological traceability, preregistration, bounded targets, field contingencies, safety, and contribution interpretation.

reports.compared_only: Compared-only guidance covers question-to-method traceability, preregistered changes, operationally justified target ranges, infrastructure failures, safety precedence, and the risk of mislabeling implemented features as contributions.
reports.reference_only: Reference-only guidance covers opening clarity, research-question formulation, procedure visuals, phased scheduling, contribution placement, reusable subheadings, and nearby feasibility evidence.
